# Discussion

Across a matched national design and multiple independent estimators, the operational effect of
reservoirs on drought brackets zero once siting is matched out. Dammed basins hold about 4.6
times more cropland than matched controls, but that gap is fixed across the record, with parallel
pre-trends and no megadrought divergence. One reading fits:
reservoirs mark where water-dependent vulnerability already concentrated, in arid, cultivated
basins, rather than make it. This is a finding, not a failure of power: the apparent effect has an
identified cause, and the positive control shows the design detects buffering. The placebo is the cleanest
falsification: a regulation effect must appear below the dam and be absent above it, and it is not;
what remains is the aridity gradient.

The corollary is transferable: dammed-versus-undammed or before-after contrasts inherit the
full siting confound
[@lopezmoreno_dam_2009; @wu_non-linear_2017; @schilstra_effects_2024; @lee_drought_2026]. The
upstream placebo ports to regulated rivers with gauges above and below a dam, most directly to
short, steep catchments like Chile's; in large low-gradient basins, longer transit,
floodplain storage and transmission losses would blur the up/down contrast, and porting it there
would need routing-corrected lags, naturalized-flow counterfactuals, or synthetic gauges built from
unregulated tributaries.

If reservoirs neither buffer nor amplify multi-year drought operationally, what matters
under a multi-decadal dry spell is the water available to store. The storage band steps down at the
megadrought onset, peak and trough together, while the amplitude trend is too imprecise to
determine whether buffering capacity degraded. The powered result is the level decline, the expected mass-balance outcome of persistent
inflow deficits; descriptive and confounded with management change, it supports no causal
attribution but is commensurate with the independent decline in unregulated control
streamflow. Read against Chile's structural aridification
[@zambrano_drought_2025; @garreaud_20102015_2017; @AlvarezGarreton2021] and the global pattern of
reservoirs failing to refill
[@wang_reservoir_2024; @li_diminishing_2023], the binding constraint is shifting toward supply.

These findings give the contested socio-hydrological *reservoir effect* and *supply-demand cycle*
[@di_baldassarre_water_2018; @kellner_controversial_2021] a credibly
identified test, and find the protective function over-attributed to storage. Because treatment is
time-invariant, we test the spatial imprint of these feedbacks, not the
longitudinal loop: the 4.6-fold cropland gap could be the equilibrated legacy of
demand induced at construction, before our record, so the null scopes to the megadrought era rather
than ruling out historical induced demand, testable only with staggered
commissioning. The window also observes only the scarcity phase of the cycle, when expansion is
constrained; the expansion phase unfolds under perceived abundance, before our record, so the null
bounds drought-era expansion, not the cycle as a whole. Within that scope the
nulls refine the theory: the supply-demand cycle
leaves no operational imprint during drought, so its mechanisms likely act through siting and
construction rather than operation, a distinction current
models omit. How far the demand-side null
travels depends on governance: the siting lesson holds wherever dams are placed non-randomly,
but prior appropriation, with forfeiture of unused rights, may amplify induced demand and
adaptive state allocation can curtail it, so the reservoir effect is
governance-mediated, not universal. Whether the demand null is general or the mark of a fully
allocated market at a hard supply ceiling we cannot adjudicate: rights kept accruing in dammed
basins, arguing against a binding ceiling, though unallocated systems could express induced demand
ours cannot.

Chile's 1981 Water Code makes water-use rights perpetual private
property, so the reflexive response has been supply-side, new dams and
inter-basin transfers [@Barria2021; @Garreaud2025]; the 2022 reform moves
toward the adaptive allocation our results argue for
[@macpherson_evolving_2023], though it postdates our window. Under
structural aridification, building more storage is a supply-blind
response to a supply problem: the buffering dams provide is a property of where they sit, not of
what they do [@ho_future_2017]. Adaptation must shift toward demand management,
reallocation and managed aquifer recharge [@grafton_paradox_2018; @scanlon_global_2023].

Several limitations bound these conclusions, each quantified in the Supplementary
Information. The result is a bounded null, not a proven
equivalence: the design excludes streamflow buffering above 46 to 59% of baseline,
demand-side outcomes are far less powered and the cropland pre-trend test is power-limited
(Supplementary Tables S2 and S14), so the causal weight rests on
the placebo, with the demand nulls corroborating; all survive the hard-balanced match
(Supplementary Table S17). Cropland area and the registry miss intensification, thirstier
crops or deeper irrigation within an unchanged footprint and entitlement stock; a
consumption-grade test awaits thermal ET or crop-transition maps.
Groundwater substitution is bounded, dammed and control water tables fall at indistinguishable
rates across 213 DGA wells despite the region's severe drawdown [@Taucare2024], though
monitored wells need not sample the orchard footprints or strata where pumping concentrates;
unmonitored drawdown could thus sustain a historically reservoir-induced footprint, a
pathway the basin bound cannot close (Supplementary Table S10). The snowmelt confound in the placebo, acute in
these snow-fed Andean basins [@ayala_glaciers_2025;
@gotte_hydrological_2024], is tested on the differential estimand itself: the up/down equivalence
survives a forcing-by-snowpack adjustment, persists among low-snow units, does not strengthen in
high-snow years, and shows no early-late divergence (Supplementary Table S12). Elevation is
only a proxy for the longitudinal profile: downstream reaches differ in channel morphology,
floodplain width, alluvial exchange and transmission losses; a residual
geomorphological contrast beyond the elevation bound cannot be excluded. Administrative closure cannot force the demand null, treated basins entered the drought with
higher allocated stock yet accrued rights 2.7 times faster, and the
parallel control cropland trajectory contradicts collapse prevention
(Supplementary Table S15). No matched pair shares a watershed; transfers out of dammed basins would
shrink the gap, and imports would mimic downstream-specific buffering, which is
absent (Supplementary Table S15); the irrigation-only
restriction leaves the result unchanged (Supplementary Table S11). MOD16's bias toward the null excludes the ET pathway from evidence
(Results; Supplementary Table S21); the demand conclusion rests on cropland and the registry, with
a thermal ET sensitivity (Landsat or ECOSTRESS class) as future work. Finally, the 12-month accumulation targets multi-year
vulnerability, not the sub-seasonal buffering reservoirs also provide, which we neither
test nor dispute. Two extensions can test what our window cannot: a staggered event study of
cropland around historical commissioning, feasible with the Landsat archive and agricultural
censuses, would probe construction-phase induced demand; a
rule-curve quasi-experiment on release records, once public, would isolate operation.

Returning to the motivating question, at the multi-year timescale of structural aridification
reservoirs neither create resilience nor postpone vulnerability operationally: storage neither
buffers nor amplifies the drought signal beyond what siting implies, while the water available to
store declines. These nulls are bounds, not zeros; effects inside them can be
volumetrically material for managers (Supplementary Table S16). Resilience to a falling
supply ceiling will come from confronting demand and
allocation, not from more impoundments.
